chapters.title: Measurement and Practical Work
chapters.description: How scientists measure, the scientific method, units, significant figures, errors, accuracy, precision, and writing clear lab reports.

lessons.title: Measurement, Uncertainty and the Scientific Method
lessons.summary: Learn the steps of the scientific method and how to record measurements with the right units, significant figures, and uncertainty. Also see the difference between accuracy and precision.

sections.title: Why measurement matters
sections.body:
Physics is built on careful **measurement**. Whether you are timing a falling stone in your school yard in Addis Ababa or measuring the current in a circuit, your conclusion is only as good as your numbers.

Scientists do not just guess. They follow the **scientific method**: a clear, evidence-based way of asking and answering questions. Every measurement also carries some **uncertainty** — a small amount of doubt. Learning to record and report this honestly is what separates real science from guessing.

sections.title: What you will be able to do
sections.body:
By the end of this lesson you should be able to:

- State the steps of the **scientific method**.
- Choose **appropriate units** for a quantity and use SI prefixes.
- Count **significant figures** and round answers correctly.
- State the **uncertainty** in a single reading and find **percentage uncertainty**.
- Tell the difference between **random** and **systematic** errors.
- Explain the difference between **accuracy** and **precision**.

sections.title: Method, units, significant figures and uncertainty
sections.body:
**The scientific method** is a repeating cycle: ask a question, do background research, form a **hypothesis** (a testable idea), make predictions, design and run an **experiment**, analyse the data, then draw conclusions. If the data does not support the hypothesis, you form a new one and try again. *Why this order?* Because only ideas that survive careful, repeatable testing — checked by other scientists (**peer review**) — can be trusted.

**SI units and prefixes.** The international system (SI) uses base units such as the **metre (m)**, **kilogram (kg)** and **second (s)**. Prefixes scale them: kilo- (×10³), centi- (×10⁻²), milli- (×10⁻³), micro- (×10⁻⁶). Choose a unit that suits the size of the thing: a seed in millimetres, a football pitch in metres.

**Significant figures (s.f.).** These are the digits that carry real information. All non-zero digits count. In 0.008 there is **one** s.f. (the zeros only show size). Trailing zeros after a decimal point (as in 3.200) **do** count. *Rule for calculations:* your answer can be no more precise than your least precise measurement. If you divide 4.345 m (4 s.f.) by 1.2 s (2 s.f.), the answer must be given to **2 s.f.**

**Uncertainty.** Every measurement has a range of doubt. Writing 1.80 m really means the value lies between 1.795 m and 1.805 m, i.e. **1.80 m ± 0.005 m**. The **percentage uncertainty** is the uncertainty divided by the reading, ×100. *Why it matters:* a small absolute uncertainty on a small reading can still be a large percentage. Measuring many items together (e.g. the thickness of 10 sheets of paper) keeps the same absolute uncertainty but cuts the percentage uncertainty. When you **combine** measurements by multiplying or dividing, you **add their percentage uncertainties**.

**Errors.** A **random error** has no pattern — it pushes readings above and below the true value, so **averaging many readings** reduces it. A **systematic error** has a bias — it pushes every reading the same way (too high or too low); averaging does **not** help. A **zero error** (an instrument that does not read zero when it should) is a common systematic error.

**Accuracy vs precision.** **Accuracy** means how close a reading is to the **true value**. **Precision** means how close repeated readings are to **each other** (little spread). They are different: a faulty ammeter can be very precise (same answer every time) yet inaccurate (biased away from the truth).

sections.title: Worked example: resistance from p.d. and current
sections.body:
**Problem:** A student measures the potential difference across a resistor as **4.32 V ± 0.05 V** and the current through it as **2.3 A ± 0.1 A**. Find the resistance and its uncertainty.

**Step 1 — Find the resistance.** Use `R = V / I`:
`R = 4.32 V / 2.3 A = 1.878... Ω`
The current has only **2 s.f.**, so round the resistance to **2 s.f.**: `R = 1.9 Ω`.

**Step 2 — Find the percentage uncertainty in each reading.**
Voltage: `(0.05 / 4.32) × 100 = 1.16 %`
Current: `(0.1 / 2.3) × 100 = 4.35 %`

**Step 3 — Combine.** Because resistance is V divided by I, **add the percentage uncertainties**:
`1.16 % + 4.35 % = 5.5 %` (2 s.f.)

**Step 4 — Convert back to an absolute uncertainty.**
`5.5 % of 1.9 Ω = 0.10 Ω`
So the result is **R = 1.9 Ω ± 0.1 Ω** (or 1.9 Ω ± 5.5 %).

**Check:** The biggest source of doubt is the current (4.35 %), and it dominates the final 5.5 % — which makes sense.

sections.title: Accuracy versus precision
sections.body: Think of shots at a target. The bullseye is the **true value**. **Accurate** shots cluster around the bullseye. **Precise** shots cluster tightly together — but if they are off-centre they are precise yet **not** accurate (a sign of a systematic error). The diagram below shows the four cases.

Top-right 'Precise but inaccurate': dots tightly grouped together but far from the bullseye (off to one side). Bottom-left 'Neither': dots scattered widely and off-centre. Bottom-right 'Accurate and precise': dots tightly grouped on the bullseye. Caption: precision = small spread; accuracy = close to the true centre.

sections.title: Mistakes students often make
sections.body:
- **Confusing accuracy and precision.** Precise means readings agree with each other; accurate means they agree with the true value.
- **Quoting too many figures.** A calculator shows 3.333333 Ω, but you may only keep as many s.f. as your least precise reading allows.
- **Counting leading zeros as significant.** In 0.008 only the 8 is significant; the zeros just show place value.
- **Thinking repeats fix systematic errors.** Averaging only reduces **random** errors. A zero error stays no matter how many times you repeat.
- **Rounding too early.** Keep all digits through the middle of a calculation and round only at the very end.
- **Forgetting units or labels** in tables — every column needs a quantity and a unit.

sections.title: Tricks to remember it
sections.body:
- **"Random Rambles, Systematic Sticks."** Random errors wander above and below; systematic errors stick to one side.
- **"AverAge Away rAndom."** Averaging only helps **random** error.
- **Accuracy = Aim at the truth; Precision = Pin them together.** Both start with the right idea.
- For combining uncertainties when you **multiply or divide**, remember **"% adds up."**
- To count significant figures, **ignore leading zeros, keep trailing decimal zeros.**

sections.title: Practice questions
sections.body:
Try these, then check the answers below.

**Q1.** How many significant figures are in (a) 258, (b) 0.084, (c) 3.200?

**Q2.** A length is measured as 12.0 cm ± 0.1 cm. What is the percentage uncertainty?

**Q3.** A current is 3.2 A ± 0.1 A and a p.d. is 12.3 V ± 0.1 V. Find the resistance and its percentage uncertainty.

**Answers:**
- **A1.** (a) 3, (b) 2, (c) 4.
- **A2.** `(0.1 / 12.0) × 100 =` **0.83 %**.
- **A3.** `R = 12.3 / 3.2 = 3.8 Ω` (2 s.f.). Percentages: current `3.1 %`, voltage `0.81 %`; total ≈ **3.9 %**, so R = 3.8 Ω ± 0.15 Ω.

sections.title: Key points
sections.body:
- The **scientific method**: question → research → hypothesis → prediction → experiment → analysis → conclusion, confirmed by **peer review**.
- Use **SI units** and prefixes suited to the size of the quantity.
- Keep answers to the correct number of **significant figures**; round only at the end.
- Every measurement has an **uncertainty**; when multiplying or dividing, **add percentage uncertainties**.
- **Random errors** are reduced by averaging; **systematic errors** (including zero errors) are not.
- **Accuracy** = close to the true value; **precision** = repeated readings close together.

sections.title: Key words
sections.body: Important terms from this lesson.

glossary.definition: A proposed, testable explanation for an observation.
The digits in a measurement that carry real information about its precision.
The amount of doubt in a measurement, e.g. 1.80 m ± 0.005 m.
An unpredictable error with no bias; it makes readings vary above and below the true value.
An error with a fixed bias that pushes every reading the same way (too high or too low).
How close a measurement is to the true value.
How close repeated measurements are to one another.

flashcards.front: List the steps of the scientific method.
flashcards.back: Ask a question, research, form a hypothesis, make predictions, experiment, analyse data, draw conclusions (then repeat if needed).

flashcards.front: How many significant figures are in 0.008?
flashcards.back: One. Leading zeros only show place value and are not significant.

flashcards.front: When you multiply or divide measurements, how do their uncertainties combine?
flashcards.back: You add the percentage uncertainties.

flashcards.front: Which type of error is reduced by taking many readings and averaging?
flashcards.back: Random error. Systematic errors are not reduced by averaging.

flashcards.front: What is the difference between accuracy and precision?
flashcards.back: Accuracy is closeness to the true value; precision is how tightly repeated readings agree with each other.

questions.prompt: What is a hypothesis in the scientific method?
options: A proven fact accepted by all scientists
A testable proposed explanation for an observation
The final conclusion of an experiment
questions.explanation: A hypothesis is a testable idea that might explain an observation; it must be tested by experiment before it can be accepted.

questions.prompt: How many significant figures does the number 0.084 have?
questions.explanation: Leading zeros are not significant; only the 8 and the 4 carry information, giving two significant figures.

questions.prompt: An ammeter always reads 0.4 A too low. What kind of error is this?
questions.explanation: A constant bias in one direction is a systematic error; here it is a zero error, and averaging readings will not remove it.

questions.prompt: A length is 20.0 cm ± 0.2 cm. What is its percentage uncertainty?
questions.explanation: Percentage uncertainty = (0.2 / 20.0) × 100 = 1.0 %.

questions.prompt: Resistance is found from R = V/I. If V has 2 % uncertainty and I has 3 % uncertainty, what is the uncertainty in R?
questions.explanation: When dividing, percentage uncertainties add: 2 % + 3 % = 5 %.

questions.prompt: A set of readings is tightly grouped together but all clearly far from the true value. How are these readings best described?
questions.explanation: Tightly grouped means precise; being far from the true value means inaccurate, which usually points to a systematic error.

chapters.title: Vector Quantities
chapters.description: The difference between scalars and vectors, how to resolve vectors into components, add and subtract them, and multiply them using the dot and cross products.

lessons.title: Vectors: Resolution, Addition and Multiplication
lessons.summary: Learn how to break vectors into components, add them tip-to-tail, and combine them with the scalar (dot) and vector (cross) products. Includes right-angle resolution with sine and cosine.

sections.title: Why vectors?
sections.body:
Some quantities need only a size, like the mass of a sack of teff (50 kg). These are **scalars**. Others need a size **and** a direction — like telling a friend to walk 3 km **north-east**. These are **vectors**.

Force, velocity, acceleration and displacement are all vectors. If you ignore direction, your physics will be wrong. This lesson shows how to handle vectors properly: splitting them up, adding them, and multiplying them.

sections.title: What you will be able to do
sections.body:
By the end of this lesson you should be able to:

- Tell the difference between a **scalar** and a **vector**.
- **Resolve** a vector into horizontal and vertical components.
- Add and subtract vectors using the **tip-to-tail** method and components.
- Find the **resultant** magnitude and direction.
- Use the **scalar (dot) product** and the **vector (cross) product**.

sections.title: Scalars, components and products
sections.body:
**Scalars vs vectors.** A **scalar** has magnitude only (mass, time, temperature, speed). A **vector** has magnitude *and* direction (displacement, velocity, force). We draw a vector as an arrow: length = size, arrowhead = direction.

**Resolving a vector.** Any vector **A** at an angle θ to the horizontal can be split into two perpendicular **components** that, added together, give the same effect:
- Horizontal: `Aₓ = A cos θ`
- Vertical: `A_y = A sin θ`
*Why this works:* the component along a direction is the "shadow" of the vector on that axis, and trigonometry of the right-angled triangle gives cos for the adjacent side and sin for the opposite side.

**Adding vectors.** Vectors add **tip-to-tail**: draw the first arrow, start the second arrow where the first ends; the **resultant** runs from the very start to the very end. The easier method for calculation is to **add components**: add all the x-parts to get Rₓ, add all the y-parts to get R_y. Then the resultant has:
- Magnitude: `R = √(Rₓ² + R_y²)` (Pythagoras)
- Direction: `θ = tan⁻¹(R_y / Rₓ)`

**Subtracting vectors.** To do **A − B**, reverse B (turn its arrow around) and add: `A + (−B)`.

**Two ways to multiply vectors.**
1. **Scalar (dot) product:** `A · B = A B cos θ`. The result is a **scalar**. It is largest when the vectors point the same way (θ = 0) and zero when they are perpendicular (θ = 90°). Work done, `W = F·d`, uses the dot product.
2. **Vector (cross) product:** `A × B = A B sin θ`, and the result is a **vector** pointing perpendicular to both A and B (direction given by the right-hand rule). It is zero when the vectors are parallel and largest when they are perpendicular. Torque, `τ = r × F`, uses the cross product.

sections.title: Worked example: resultant of two forces
sections.body:
**Problem:** Two forces act on a box: **3.0 N due east** and **4.0 N due north**. Find the magnitude and direction of the resultant.

**Step 1 — Choose axes.** Let east = +x and north = +y.
`Rₓ = 3.0 N`, `R_y = 4.0 N`.

**Step 2 — Find the magnitude.** Use Pythagoras:
`R = √(Rₓ² + R_y²) = √(3.0² + 4.0²) = √(9 + 16) = √25 = 5.0 N`

**Step 3 — Find the direction.** Measure the angle north of east:
`θ = tan⁻¹(R_y / Rₓ) = tan⁻¹(4.0 / 3.0) = tan⁻¹(1.33) = 53°`

**Answer:** The resultant is **5.0 N at 53° north of east**.

**Check:** 3-4-5 is a classic right triangle, so 5.0 N is exactly right, and the larger force (north) means the angle should lean toward north — it does.

sections.title: Resolving a force into components
sections.body: The free-body sketch below shows a single force **F** acting at angle θ above the horizontal, split into its horizontal part `F cos θ` and its vertical part `F sin θ`. Together the two components make a right-angled triangle whose hypotenuse is F.

data.description: A point with one arrow labelled F pointing up and to the right at angle theta from the horizontal. A horizontal dashed arrow along the x-axis labelled 'F cos theta' and a vertical dashed arrow along the y-axis labelled 'F sin theta' form a right-angled triangle with F as the hypotenuse. The angle theta is marked between F and the horizontal.

sections.title: Mistakes students often make
sections.body:
- **Adding magnitudes directly.** 3 N + 4 N is **not** 7 N unless the forces point the same way. Use components or the tip-to-tail rule.
- **Swapping sin and cos.** The component **along** the angle's adjacent side uses **cos**; the opposite side uses **sin**.
- **Mixing up the products.** The **dot** product gives a scalar (cos); the **cross** product gives a vector (sin).
- **Forgetting direction.** A vector answer is incomplete without its angle or direction.
- **Sign errors in subtraction.** To subtract a vector, reverse it first, then add.

sections.title: Tricks to remember it
sections.body:
- **"Dot is Down-to-earth (scalar), Cross is a Crossing arrow (vector)."** The dot product gives a number; the cross product gives a new vector.
- **"Dot uses cos, Cross uses sin"** — both have an 'o-s' link: cOS with dot, Sin with cross? Use the rhyme: *"Cosine for the dot, sine for the not."*
- For components, picture the **shadow**: the horizontal shadow is `A cos θ`, the vertical shadow is `A sin θ`.
- **"Tip to tail, follow the trail"** for adding vectors head-to-tail.
- A **3-4-5** triangle gives a resultant of 5 — a handy check.

sections.title: Practice questions
sections.body:
Try these, then check the answers below.

**Q1.** A velocity of 10 m/s points at 30° above the horizontal. Find its horizontal and vertical components.

**Q2.** Two displacements, 6.0 m east and 8.0 m north, are added. What is the magnitude of the resultant?

**Q3.** Two forces of 5 N each act on a point at 90° to each other. Find their scalar (dot) product.

**Answers:**
- **A1.** Horizontal `= 10 cos 30° = 8.7 m/s`; vertical `= 10 sin 30° = 5.0 m/s`.
- **A2.** `R = √(6.0² + 8.0²) = √(36 + 64) = √100 =` **10 m**.
- **A3.** `A·B = A B cos 90° = 5 × 5 × 0 =` **0** (perpendicular vectors have zero dot product).

sections.title: Key points
sections.body:
- A **scalar** has size only; a **vector** has size **and** direction.
- Resolve a vector: `Aₓ = A cos θ`, `A_y = A sin θ`.
- Add vectors **tip-to-tail** or by adding components; resultant `R = √(Rₓ² + R_y²)`, direction `θ = tan⁻¹(R_y/Rₓ)`.
- To subtract, **reverse** the second vector and add.
- **Dot product** `A·B = AB cos θ` gives a **scalar**; **cross product** `A×B = AB sin θ` gives a **vector**.

sections.title: Key words
sections.body: Important terms from this lesson.

glossary.definition: A quantity with magnitude only, such as mass, time or speed.
A quantity with both magnitude and direction, such as force or velocity.
The part of a vector along a chosen axis, found using sine or cosine.
The single vector that has the same effect as two or more vectors added together.
A·B = AB cos θ; the result is a scalar.
A×B = AB sin θ; the result is a vector perpendicular to both.

flashcards.front: What is the difference between a scalar and a vector?
flashcards.back: A scalar has magnitude only; a vector has both magnitude and direction.

flashcards.front: How do you resolve a vector A at angle θ into components?
flashcards.back: Horizontal Aₓ = A cos θ; vertical A_y = A sin θ.

flashcards.front: How do you find the magnitude of a resultant from its components?
flashcards.back: R = √(Rₓ² + R_y²) using Pythagoras.

flashcards.front: What does the scalar (dot) product give and how is it found?
flashcards.back: It gives a scalar: A·B = A B cos θ.

flashcards.front: What does the vector (cross) product give and how is it found?
flashcards.back: It gives a vector perpendicular to both, with magnitude A·B sin θ.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is a vector quantity?
questions.explanation: Velocity has both magnitude and direction, so it is a vector. Mass, temperature and time are scalars.

questions.prompt: A force F acts at angle θ above the horizontal. What is its horizontal component?
questions.explanation: The horizontal (adjacent) component is F cos θ; the vertical (opposite) component is F sin θ.

questions.prompt: Two perpendicular forces of 3 N and 4 N act on a point. What is the magnitude of the resultant?
questions.explanation: R = √(3² + 4²) = √25 = 5 N. You cannot simply add 3 + 4 because the forces are perpendicular.

questions.prompt: Two vectors are perpendicular. What is their scalar (dot) product?
questions.explanation: A·B = AB cos 90° = 0, because cos 90° = 0. The dot product is zero for perpendicular vectors.

questions.prompt: For which angle between two vectors is the magnitude of the cross product greatest?
questions.explanation: |A×B| = AB sin θ is greatest when sin θ = 1, i.e. when θ = 90° (the vectors are perpendicular).

questions.prompt: A resultant has components Rₓ = 6 N and R_y = 6 N. What angle does it make with the x-axis?
questions.explanation: θ = tan⁻¹(R_y/Rₓ) = tan⁻¹(6/6) = tan⁻¹(1) = 45°.

chapters.title: Kinematics
chapters.description: Describing motion in a straight line and in a plane using displacement, velocity, acceleration, the equations of motion, and projectile motion.

lessons.title: Motion in a Straight Line and in a Plane
lessons.summary: Learn the equations of uniformly accelerated motion and how to read motion graphs. Then extend to projectile motion in a plane by treating horizontal and vertical motion separately.

sections.title: Describing how things move
sections.body:
**Kinematics** is the study of motion without worrying about what causes it. When a bus pulls away from a stop in Bahir Dar, or a stone is thrown into Lake Tana, we can describe exactly where it is and how fast it moves using a few powerful equations.

We start with motion in a **straight line** (1D), then move to motion in a **plane** (2D), such as a thrown ball that moves forward and falls at the same time.

sections.title: What you will be able to do
sections.body:
By the end of this lesson you should be able to:

- Define **displacement**, **velocity** and **acceleration**.
- Use the **equations of uniformly accelerated motion**.
- Read and interpret **displacement-time** and **velocity-time** graphs.
- Explain that horizontal and vertical motion are **independent**.
- Solve **projectile** problems for time, range and height.

sections.title: Equations of motion and projectiles
sections.body:
**Key quantities.** **Displacement (s)** is the straight-line distance and direction from start to finish (a vector). **Velocity (v)** is the rate of change of displacement (a vector). **Acceleration (a)** is the rate of change of velocity. *Speed* and *distance* are the scalar cousins that ignore direction.

**Equations of uniformly accelerated motion** (constant acceleration). With u = initial velocity, v = final velocity, a = acceleration, s = displacement, t = time:
1. `v = u + at`
2. `s = ½(u + v)t`
3. `s = ut + ½at²`
4. `v² = u² + 2as`
*Why so many?* Each equation leaves out one variable, so you pick the one that contains the three things you know plus the one you want.

**Reading motion graphs.** On a **displacement-time** graph the **gradient (slope) = velocity**. On a **velocity-time** graph the **gradient = acceleration**, and the **area under the line = displacement**. A straight sloping velocity-time line means constant acceleration.

**Motion in a plane (projectiles).** A **projectile** moves under gravity only. The big idea is **independence of motion**: the horizontal and vertical parts happen together but do not affect each other.
- **Horizontal:** no force (ignoring air resistance), so velocity is **constant**: `x = uₓ t`.
- **Vertical:** gravity gives `a = g = 9.81 m/s²` downward, so the vertical velocity changes; use the equations of motion with a = g.

Resolve a launch velocity u at angle θ: `uₓ = u cos θ`, `u_y = u sin θ`. The path is a **parabola**. Useful ground-to-ground results: time to top `t = u sin θ / g`, total time `T = 2u sin θ / g`, range `R = u² sin 2θ / g`, with maximum range at **θ = 45°**.

sections.title: Worked example: a decelerating car
sections.body:
**Problem:** A car travelling at **30 m/s** brakes with a constant acceleration of **−5.0 m/s²**. (a) How long does it take to stop? (b) How far does it travel while stopping?

**Step 1 — List what you know.** `u = 30 m/s`, `v = 0` (stops), `a = −5.0 m/s²`.

**Step 2 — Find the time.** Use `v = u + at`:
`0 = 30 + (−5.0)t`
`5.0 t = 30`
`t = 6.0 s`

**Step 3 — Find the stopping distance.** Use `v² = u² + 2as`:
`0 = 30² + 2(−5.0)s`
`0 = 900 − 10 s`
`s = 900 / 10 = 90 m`

**Answer:** It stops in **6.0 s** after travelling **90 m**.

**Check:** Average velocity `= (30 + 0)/2 = 15 m/s`; distance `= 15 × 6.0 = 90 m`. The two methods agree.

sections.title: Velocity-time graph of the braking car
sections.body: The line starts at 30 m/s and falls steadily to 0 at 6 seconds. The straight line shows **constant deceleration**. The triangular **area under the line** equals the distance travelled: `½ × 6.0 s × 30 m/s = 90 m`, matching the worked example.

sections.title: Mistakes students often make
sections.body:
- **Confusing distance and displacement.** Displacement is the straight-line vector from start to finish; distance is the total path length.
- **Sign errors.** Deceleration and downward gravity are **negative** if you choose forward/up as positive. Stay consistent.
- **Using full speed for vertical work.** For a launch at an angle, the vertical part is `u sin θ`, not the full u.
- **Reading the wrong graph quantity.** On a velocity-time graph the slope is acceleration and the area is displacement — not the other way round.
- **Thinking horizontal velocity drops.** In projectile motion the horizontal velocity stays constant (no air resistance).

sections.title: Tricks to remember it
sections.body:
- **"suvat"** lists the five symbols (s, u, v, a, t). Pick the equation that contains the three you know and the one you want.
- On graphs: **"slope and area"** — *velocity-time: slope = a, area = s.*
- **"45 is the king of range"** — the longest flat-ground range is at 45°.
- **"Time up = time down"** for a projectile that lands at its launch height.
- For vertical/horizontal split, recall **sin for up, cos across** (`u sin θ` vertical, `u cos θ` horizontal).

sections.title: Practice questions
sections.body:
Try these, then check the answers below.

**Q1.** A stone is dropped from rest. How fast is it moving after 2.0 s? (g = 9.81 m/s².)

**Q2.** A ball is thrown horizontally at 12 m/s from a cliff. How far does it travel horizontally in 3.0 s?

**Q3.** A car accelerates from 10 m/s to 25 m/s in 5.0 s. What is its acceleration?

**Answers:**
- **A1.** `v = u + gt = 0 + 9.81 × 2.0 =` **19.6 m/s** downward.
- **A2.** `x = uₓ t = 12 × 3.0 =` **36 m**.
- **A3.** `a = (v − u)/t = (25 − 10)/5.0 = 15/5.0 =` **3.0 m/s²**.

sections.title: Key points
sections.body:
- **Displacement, velocity and acceleration** are vectors; speed and distance are scalars.
- Use the **four equations of motion** for constant acceleration; choose the one with your known and wanted variables.
- On a **velocity-time graph**: slope = acceleration, area = displacement.
- A **projectile** has constant **horizontal** velocity and changing **vertical** velocity (a = g).
- Resolve launch velocity: `uₓ = u cos θ`, `u_y = u sin θ`; **maximum range at 45°**.

sections.title: Key words
sections.body: Important terms from this lesson.

glossary.definition: The straight-line distance and direction from the start point to the end point.
The rate of change of displacement; a vector.
The rate of change of velocity.
An object moving through the air under the influence of gravity alone.
The curved path followed by a projectile.
The horizontal distance a projectile travels before landing at its launch height.

flashcards.front: What is the difference between distance and displacement?
flashcards.back: Distance is total path length (scalar); displacement is the straight-line distance and direction from start to finish (vector).

flashcards.front: On a velocity-time graph, what do the slope and the area represent?
flashcards.back: The slope is acceleration; the area under the line is displacement.

flashcards.front: Which equation links v, u, a and s without time?
flashcards.back: v² = u² + 2as.

flashcards.front: Why does horizontal velocity stay constant for a projectile?
flashcards.back: Ignoring air resistance, there is no horizontal force, so no horizontal acceleration.

flashcards.front: At what launch angle is the range greatest on flat ground?
flashcards.back: 45°, where R = u² / g.

questions.prompt: Which equation correctly relates final velocity v, initial velocity u, acceleration a and time t?
questions.explanation: v = u + at is the first equation of uniformly accelerated motion.

questions.prompt: On a velocity-time graph, what does the gradient (slope) represent?
questions.explanation: The slope of a velocity-time graph is the rate of change of velocity, which is acceleration.

questions.prompt: A stone is dropped from rest. What is its speed after 3.0 s? (g = 9.81 m/s²)
For a ball launched at 20 m/s and 30°, what is the vertical component of the launch velocity?
questions.explanation: Vertical component = u sin θ = 20 × sin 30° = 20 × 0.5 = 10 m/s.

chapters.title: Dynamics
chapters.description: Forces and Newton's laws of motion, momentum and its conservation, collisions, centre of mass, and the dynamics of circular motion.

lessons.title: Newton's Laws, Momentum and Circular Motion
lessons.summary: Learn Newton's three laws of motion, the principle of conservation of momentum, and how forces cause circular motion. Includes collisions and centripetal force.

sections.title: What makes things move?
sections.body:
**Dynamics** asks *why* objects move the way they do. The answer is **force**. A push, a pull, friction, gravity, tension — all are forces, and they change motion.

**Sir Isaac Newton** summed up the rules in three short laws. Together with the idea of **momentum**, they explain everything from a kicked ball to a satellite circling the Earth.

sections.title: What you will be able to do
sections.body:
By the end of this lesson you should be able to:

- State and use **Newton's three laws of motion**.
- Calculate **force** using F = ma.
- Define **momentum** and apply the **law of conservation of momentum**.
- Tell **elastic** from **inelastic** collisions.
- Explain **centripetal force** and calculate it with F = mv²/r.

sections.title: Newton's laws, momentum and circular motion
sections.body:
**Newton's first law (inertia).** An object stays at rest, or keeps moving at constant velocity, **unless a net (resultant) force acts on it**. *Why:* objects have **inertia** — a natural resistance to changes in motion. A book on a table stays put because the forces balance.

**Newton's second law.** The net force equals the rate of change of momentum, which for constant mass gives:
`F = ma`
Force in newtons (N), mass in kg, acceleration in m/s². *Why:* a bigger force gives a bigger acceleration, but a heavier object accelerates less for the same force.

**Newton's third law.** For every action there is an **equal and opposite reaction**. If you push on a wall, the wall pushes back on you with the same force. The two forces act on **different objects**.

**Momentum.** **Momentum** is mass × velocity: `p = mv` (a vector, in kg·m/s). A heavy, fast object has large momentum.

**Conservation of momentum.** In a closed system (no outside forces), the **total momentum before = total momentum after**:
`m₁u₁ + m₂u₂ = m₁v₁ + m₂v₂`
*Why:* it follows directly from Newton's third law — the forces in a collision are equal and opposite, so the momentum one object loses the other gains.

**Collisions.** In an **elastic** collision both momentum **and** kinetic energy are conserved (e.g. ideal billiard balls). In an **inelastic** collision momentum is conserved but **kinetic energy is not** — some becomes heat or sound. If objects stick together, it is **perfectly inelastic**.

**Circular motion.** An object moving in a circle at constant speed is still **accelerating**, because its **direction** (and so its velocity) keeps changing. This needs an inward **centripetal force** pointing to the centre:
`F = mv² / r`
where m = mass, v = speed, r = radius. For a car rounding a bend this force is friction; for a satellite it is gravity. There is **no outward 'centrifugal force'** acting on the object — the feeling of being thrown outward is just inertia.

sections.title: Worked example: a perfectly inelastic collision
sections.body:
**Problem:** A **2.0 kg** trolley moving at **3.0 m/s** collides with a stationary **1.0 kg** trolley and they stick together. Find their common velocity after the collision.

**Step 1 — Write the conservation of momentum equation.** Before, only the first trolley moves:
`m₁u₁ + m₂u₂ = (m₁ + m₂)v`

**Step 2 — Put in the numbers.**
`(2.0 × 3.0) + (1.0 × 0) = (2.0 + 1.0) × v`
`6.0 + 0 = 3.0 v`

**Step 3 — Solve for v.**
`v = 6.0 / 3.0 = 2.0 m/s`

**Answer:** They move off together at **2.0 m/s** in the original direction.

**Check kinetic energy:** Before = `½ × 2.0 × 3.0² = 9.0 J`; after = `½ × 3.0 × 2.0² = 6.0 J`. Kinetic energy fell from 9.0 J to 6.0 J, confirming this collision is **inelastic** (some energy became heat and sound).

sections.title: Forces on a box being pulled
sections.body: The free-body diagram below shows a box on the ground. The applied pull and friction act horizontally; weight and the normal (support) force act vertically. The **net force** is what F = ma uses. When the box moves at steady speed, friction balances the pull.

data.description: A rectangular box with four force arrows. An arrow pointing right labelled 'Applied force F'. A shorter arrow pointing left labelled 'Friction f'. An arrow pointing down from the centre labelled 'Weight W = mg'. An arrow of equal length pointing up labelled 'Normal force N'. Caption: net horizontal force = F − f gives acceleration via F = ma.

sections.title: Mistakes students often make
sections.body:
- **Thinking a moving object needs a constant force.** By Newton's first law, an object keeps moving at constant velocity with **zero** net force. Force is needed only to **change** motion.
- **Putting action and reaction on the same object.** Newton's third-law pairs act on **different** objects, so they never cancel each other on one body.
- **Believing kinetic energy is always conserved.** Momentum is always conserved in a closed collision, but **kinetic energy is only conserved in elastic collisions**.
- **Inventing a 'centrifugal force'.** The real force in circular motion points **inward** (centripetal). The outward feeling is inertia, not a force on the object.
- **Forgetting that momentum is a vector.** Include direction (signs) when objects move toward each other.

sections.title: Tricks to remember it
sections.body:
- **First law = lazy law:** objects are lazy and keep doing what they were doing.
- **Second law:** **"Fame = ma"** sounds like F = ma.
- **Third law:** **"push back"** — every push gets an equal push back on you.
- **"Momentum is mass on the move"**: p = mv.
- For circular motion, chant **"mv-squared-over-r"** for centripetal force, always pointing **to the centre**.

sections.title: Practice questions
sections.body:
Try these, then check the answers below.

**Q1.** What net force is needed to give a 5.0 kg mass an acceleration of 2.0 m/s²?

**Q2.** A 1500 kg car travels at 20 m/s. What is its momentum?

**Q3.** A 0.50 kg ball is whirled in a circle of radius 0.80 m at 4.0 m/s. What centripetal force acts on it?

**Answers:**
- **A1.** `F = ma = 5.0 × 2.0 =` **10 N**.
- **A2.** `p = mv = 1500 × 20 =` **30 000 kg·m/s**.
- **A3.** `F = mv²/r = 0.50 × 4.0² / 0.80 = 0.50 × 16 / 0.80 =` **10 N**.

sections.title: Key points
sections.body:
- **Newton's first law:** no net force → no change in motion (inertia).
- **Newton's second law:** `F = ma`.
- **Newton's third law:** equal and opposite reactions on **different** objects.
- **Momentum** `p = mv` is conserved in a closed system.
- **Elastic** collisions conserve kinetic energy; **inelastic** ones do not (momentum still conserved).
- **Circular motion** needs a **centripetal force** `F = mv²/r` toward the centre.

sections.body: Important terms from this lesson.

glossary.definition: The tendency of an object to resist changes to its state of motion.
A push or pull that can change an object's motion; measured in newtons (N).
The product of mass and velocity, p = mv; a vector.
In a closed system the total momentum before equals the total momentum after.
A collision in which both momentum and kinetic energy are conserved.
The inward net force that keeps an object moving in a circle, F = mv²/r.

chapters.title: Work, Energy and Power
chapters.description: Work as a scalar product, kinetic and potential energy, the work-energy theorem, conservation of energy, and power.

lessons.title: Work, Energy and Power
lessons.summary: Learn how work transfers energy, the difference between kinetic and potential energy, the work-energy theorem, conservation of energy, and how power measures the rate of doing work.

sections.title: Energy makes things happen
sections.body:
Everything that happens — a farmer lifting a sack, a waterfall at the Blue Nile turning a turbine, a runner sprinting — involves **energy** being transferred. In physics we transfer energy by doing **work**.

This lesson links three closely related ideas: **work** (transferring energy with a force), **energy** (the capacity to do work), and **power** (how fast work is done).

sections.title: What you will be able to do
sections.body:
By the end of this lesson you should be able to:

- Define **work** and calculate it with W = Fd cos θ.
- Calculate **kinetic energy** and **gravitational potential energy**.
- Apply the **work-energy theorem**.
- State and use the **conservation of energy**.
- Define and calculate **power**.

sections.title: Work, energy and power
sections.body:
**Work.** **Work** is done when a force moves an object along the direction of the force:
`W = F d cos θ`
where F is the force, d the displacement, and θ the angle between them. Work is a **scalar** measured in **joules (J)**. *Why the cos θ?* Only the part of the force **along** the motion does work. If you carry a sack horizontally, the upward force does **no** work because θ = 90° and cos 90° = 0.

**Kinetic energy.** Energy of motion:
`KE = ½ m v²`
A faster object has much more kinetic energy because v is **squared** — double the speed gives four times the energy.

**Gravitational potential energy.** Energy stored by height:
`PE = m g h`
where h is the height raised and g = 9.81 m/s².

**The work-energy theorem.** The **net work** done on an object equals its **change in kinetic energy**:
`W_net = ΔKE = ½ m v² − ½ m u²`
*Why:* a net force accelerates the object, and accelerating it changes its speed and therefore its kinetic energy.

**Conservation of energy.** Energy cannot be created or destroyed, only **transformed** from one form to another. For a falling object (ignoring air resistance), lost potential energy becomes gained kinetic energy:
`m g h = ½ m v²`
Forces like gravity are **conservative** (energy is recoverable); forces like friction are **dissipative** (they turn useful energy into heat).

**Power.** **Power** is the rate of doing work, or the rate of transferring energy:
`P = W / t`
measured in **watts (W)**, where 1 W = 1 J/s. For a steady force moving at speed v, `P = F v`.

sections.title: Worked example: lifting a sack of grain
sections.body:
**Problem:** A worker lifts a **25 kg** sack of grain straight up onto a shelf **2.0 m** high in **4.0 s**. Take g = 9.81 m/s². Find (a) the work done and (b) the power used.

**Step 1 — Find the force needed.** To lift at steady speed, the force equals the weight:
`F = m g = 25 × 9.81 = 245.25 N`

**Step 2 — Find the work done.** The force is straight up and so is the motion, so θ = 0 and cos 0 = 1:
`W = F d = 245.25 × 2.0 = 490.5 J`
So the work done is about **490 J**. (This equals the gain in potential energy, `mgh = 25 × 9.81 × 2.0 = 490.5 J`.)

**Step 3 — Find the power.** Power is work over time:
`P = W / t = 490.5 / 4.0 = 122.6 W`
So the power is about **123 W**.

**Check:** A typical light bulb is around 60 W, so a person briefly working at ~120 W is reasonable.

sections.title: Energy transfer for a falling ball
sections.body: As a ball falls, its **potential energy** falls while its **kinetic energy** rises by the same amount, so the **total energy** stays constant (ignoring air resistance). The graph shows velocity rising as the ball speeds up — its kinetic energy (½mv²) grows as height (and PE) is lost.

sections.title: Mistakes students often make
sections.body:
- **Thinking holding something still does work.** If there is no movement (d = 0), **no work** is done, even though your muscles get tired.
- **Ignoring the angle.** Work uses the component of force **along** the motion: W = Fd cos θ. A perpendicular force does zero work.
- **Forgetting v is squared in KE.** Doubling the speed gives **four times** the kinetic energy, not twice.
- **Confusing energy and power.** Energy (J) is the total transferred; power (W) is how **fast** it is transferred.
- **Saying energy is 'used up'.** Energy is never destroyed; it is **transformed** (often into heat by friction).

sections.title: Tricks to remember it
sections.body:
- **"Work = Force along the way"** reminds you of the cos θ (force along the motion).
- **"Half-em-vee-squared"** for kinetic energy: ½mv².
- **"mgh climbs high"** for gravitational potential energy.
- **Power is energy in a hurry** — same energy, less time = more power.
- **No move, no work:** if displacement is zero, the work is zero.

sections.title: Practice questions
sections.body:
Try these, then check the answers below.

**Q1.** A force of 20 N pushes a box 5.0 m in the direction of the force. How much work is done?

**Q2.** What is the kinetic energy of a 2.0 kg ball moving at 6.0 m/s?

**Q3.** A motor does 6000 J of work in 30 s. What is its power output?

**Answers:**
- **A1.** `W = Fd = 20 × 5.0 =` **100 J**.
- **A2.** `KE = ½mv² = ½ × 2.0 × 6.0² = ½ × 2.0 × 36 =` **36 J**.
- **A3.** `P = W/t = 6000 / 30 =` **200 W**.

sections.title: Key points
sections.body:
- **Work** `W = Fd cos θ` transfers energy and is measured in **joules**.
- **Kinetic energy** `KE = ½mv²`; **potential energy** `PE = mgh`.
- The **work-energy theorem:** net work = change in kinetic energy.
- **Energy is conserved** — it is transformed, never destroyed.
- **Power** `P = W/t` (or `P = Fv`) is the rate of energy transfer, in **watts**.

sections.body: Important terms from this lesson.

The SI unit of energy and work; 1 J = 1 N·m.
The energy of a moving object, KE = ½mv².
Stored energy due to position or height, PE = mgh.
Energy cannot be created or destroyed, only transformed from one form to another.
The rate of doing work or transferring energy, P = W/t, measured in watts.

chapters.title: Rotational Motion
chapters.description: Rotation about a fixed axis, torque and angular acceleration, rotational kinetic energy and inertia, angular momentum, and its conservation.

lessons.title: Rotation, Torque and Angular Momentum
lessons.summary: Learn the angular versions of the linear quantities: angular velocity and acceleration, torque, moment of inertia, rotational kinetic energy, and the conservation of angular momentum.

sections.title: Spinning, not just sliding
sections.body:
So far motion has meant moving from place to place. But many things **spin**: a wheel, a spinning top, the blades of a water pump, even the Earth itself. This is **rotational motion**.

The good news: rotation follows the **same pattern** as straight-line motion, but with new 'angular' versions of each quantity. Once you see the matching, it becomes easy.

sections.title: What you will be able to do
sections.body:
By the end of this lesson you should be able to:

- Define **angular displacement, velocity** and **acceleration**.
- Define **torque** and calculate it with τ = rF sin θ.
- Explain **moment of inertia** and **rotational kinetic energy**.
- Use the rotational form of Newton's second law, **τ = Iα**.
- State and apply the **conservation of angular momentum**.

sections.title: Angular quantities, torque and inertia
sections.body:
**Angular quantities.** Instead of distance we measure the **angle turned**, the **angular displacement (θ)** in radians. Its rate of change is the **angular velocity (ω)** in rad/s, and the rate of change of ω is the **angular acceleration (α)** in rad/s². They link to linear quantities by the radius r: `v = rω` and `a = rα`.

**Torque.** A force makes something spin only if it acts off-centre. The turning effect is the **torque** (or moment):
`τ = r F sin θ`
where r is the distance from the axis to where the force acts, and θ is the angle between r and the force. Torque is largest when the force is **perpendicular** (θ = 90°). *Why:* pushing a door near the hinge does little; pushing far from the hinge, at right angles, turns it easily.

**Moment of inertia.** In rotation, the resistance to a change in spin is the **moment of inertia (I)**, the rotational version of mass. It depends not only on how much mass there is but on **how far that mass is from the axis** (`I = Σmr²`). Mass far from the axis is harder to spin up.

**Newton's second law for rotation.**
`τ = I α`
The net torque equals the moment of inertia times the angular acceleration — exactly mirroring F = ma.

**Rotational kinetic energy.**
`KE_rot = ½ I ω²`
the spinning version of ½mv².

**Angular momentum.** The rotational version of momentum:
`L = I ω`

**Conservation of angular momentum.** If no external torque acts, **total angular momentum stays constant**: `I₁ω₁ = I₂ω₂`. *Why it matters:* a spinning ice skater pulls her arms in, lowering I, so ω **increases** and she spins faster. The same idea explains why a diver tucks to spin quickly.

sections.title: Worked example: torque on a wheel
sections.body:
**Problem:** A force of **40 N** is applied at the edge of a wheel of radius **0.30 m**, at right angles to the radius. The wheel has a moment of inertia of **0.60 kg·m²**. Find (a) the torque and (b) the angular acceleration.

**Step 1 — Find the torque.** The force is perpendicular, so θ = 90° and sin 90° = 1:
`τ = r F sin θ = 0.30 × 40 × 1 = 12 N·m`

**Step 2 — Find the angular acceleration.** Use the rotational second law `τ = Iα`:
`α = τ / I = 12 / 0.60 = 20 rad/s²`

**Answer:** The torque is **12 N·m** and the angular acceleration is **20 rad/s²**.

**Check:** A larger force or radius would give more torque; a larger moment of inertia would give less angular acceleration — both behave as expected.

sections.title: Torque depends on where you push
sections.body: The diagram below shows a door seen from above, hinged on the left. A force applied far from the hinge, at right angles, produces a large torque (τ = rF). The same force applied near the hinge, or along the door, produces little or no torque.

data.description: Top-down view of a door hinged at the left edge (axis marked with a small circle). Three force arrows: (1) a long lever arm r to the right edge with a force arrow perpendicular to the door labelled 'large torque'; (2) a force near the hinge perpendicular to the door labelled 'small torque (small r)'; (3) a force at the far edge pointing along the door (toward the hinge) labelled 'zero torque (force parallel to r)'. Caption: torque τ = rF sin θ, greatest when the force is far out and perpendicular.

sections.title: Mistakes students often make
sections.body:
- **Ignoring where the force acts.** Torque depends on the **distance from the axis**; the same force gives more torque with a longer lever arm.
- **Forgetting the angle.** Only the perpendicular part of the force turns the object: τ = rF sin θ.
- **Treating moment of inertia like plain mass.** I depends on **how the mass is spread out**, not just how much there is.
- **Mixing linear and angular formulas.** Use ω, α, I, τ, L for rotation — not v, a, m, F, p.
- **Thinking a skater speeds up 'for no reason'.** Pulling arms in lowers I, and because L = Iω is conserved, ω must rise.

sections.title: Tricks to remember it
sections.body:
- **Rotation mirrors translation:** swap **m→I, v→ω, a→α, F→τ, p→L**. Every linear equation has a twin.
- **"Torque = turn,"** and longer lever arm = easier turn (think of a long spanner).
- **"tau = I alpha"** is the spin twin of **"F = ma."**
- **Skater spin:** arms **in** → spin **fast** (I down, ω up). Arms out → spin slow.
- Rotational KE is **"half-I-omega-squared"**, just like ½mv².

sections.title: Practice questions
sections.body:
Try these, then check the answers below.

**Q1.** A force of 25 N is applied at right angles 0.40 m from an axis. What is the torque?

**Q2.** A wheel has I = 2.0 kg·m² and spins at ω = 5.0 rad/s. What is its angular momentum?

**Q3.** A skater with I = 4.0 kg·m² spins at 2.0 rad/s, then pulls in to I = 2.0 kg·m². What is her new angular speed?

**Answers:**
- **A1.** `τ = rF sin 90° = 0.40 × 25 × 1 =` **10 N·m**.
- **A2.** `L = Iω = 2.0 × 5.0 =` **10 kg·m²/s**.
- **A3.** Conserving L: `I₁ω₁ = I₂ω₂` → `4.0 × 2.0 = 2.0 × ω₂` → ω₂ = **4.0 rad/s**.

sections.title: Key points
sections.body:
- Rotation uses **angular** quantities: θ, ω, α, linked to linear ones by `v = rω`, `a = rα`.
- **Torque** `τ = rF sin θ` is the turning effect; greatest when the force is perpendicular and far from the axis.
- **Moment of inertia (I)** is rotational mass; it depends on how mass is distributed.
- Rotational second law: `τ = Iα`; rotational KE `= ½Iω²`; angular momentum `L = Iω`.
- **Angular momentum is conserved** when no external torque acts (skater spins faster with arms in).

sections.title: Key words
sections.body: Important terms from this lesson.

glossary.definition: The rate of change of angular displacement, ω, measured in rad/s.
The turning effect of a force, τ = rF sin θ, measured in N·m.
The resistance of an object to a change in its rotation; depends on mass and its distance from the axis.
The energy of a spinning object, KE = ½Iω².
The rotational equivalent of momentum, L = Iω.
Total angular momentum stays constant when no external torque acts.

lessons.title: Equilibrium: Balanced Forces and Moments
lessons.summary: Learn the two conditions for an object to be in equilibrium: balanced forces and balanced moments. Includes the principle of moments and couples.

sections.title: Staying balanced
sections.body:
A bridge over the Awash River, a ladder leaning on a wall, a seesaw with two children — all are examples of **equilibrium**, where everything is balanced and nothing accelerates or starts to spin.

Understanding equilibrium lets engineers design safe structures. The rules are simple but powerful: the **forces must balance**, and the **turning effects must balance** too.

sections.title: What you will be able to do
sections.body:
By the end of this lesson you should be able to:

- Define **equilibrium** for a particle and a rigid body.
- State the **two conditions of equilibrium**.
- Use the **principle of moments** to solve balance problems.
- Define a **couple** and its **moment**.
- Apply equilibrium to real situations like a seesaw or beam.

sections.title: Conditions of equilibrium and moments
sections.body:
**Equilibrium of a particle.** A particle (a point object) is in equilibrium when the **net force on it is zero**, so it stays at rest or moves at constant velocity. In components: the up forces equal the down forces, and the left forces equal the right forces (`ΣFₓ = 0` and `ΣF_y = 0`).

**Moment (torque) of a force.** For a body that can rotate, we also need the turning effects to balance. The **moment** of a force about a pivot is:
`moment = force × perpendicular distance from the pivot`
measured in N·m. A clockwise moment turns one way; an anticlockwise moment turns the other.

**The two conditions of equilibrium.** A rigid body is in **complete equilibrium** only if **both** are true:
1. **The net force is zero** (no linear acceleration): `ΣF = 0`.
2. **The net moment about any point is zero** (no angular acceleration): `Στ = 0`.
*Why both?* Balanced forces stop it sliding; balanced moments stop it spinning. You need both for true balance.

**The principle of moments.** For a body balanced about a pivot:
`total clockwise moments = total anticlockwise moments`
This is just condition 2 written out. It is what makes a seesaw balance: a heavy child sits closer to the pivot, a light child sits further away.

**Couples.** A **couple** is a pair of equal, opposite, parallel forces whose lines of action do **not** pass through the same point. A couple produces **only rotation** (no net force) — think of the two hands turning a steering wheel. The **moment of a couple** is:
`moment = one force × perpendicular distance between the two forces`

sections.title: Worked example: balancing a seesaw
sections.body:
**Problem:** A child of weight **300 N** sits **1.5 m** to the left of the pivot of a seesaw. Where must a child of weight **450 N** sit on the right to balance it?

**Step 1 — Apply the principle of moments.** For balance:
`clockwise moment = anticlockwise moment`
Left child gives an anticlockwise moment; right child a clockwise moment.

**Step 2 — Write the moments.** Let the right child sit a distance d from the pivot.
`300 N × 1.5 m = 450 N × d`
`450 = 450 × d`

**Step 3 — Solve for d.**
`d = 450 / 450 = 1.0 m`

**Answer:** The 450 N child must sit **1.0 m** from the pivot.

**Check:** The heavier child sits **closer** to the pivot, which is exactly what we expect — a larger force needs a smaller distance to give the same moment.

sections.title: A balanced seesaw
sections.body: The diagram shows the seesaw from the worked example. The lighter 300 N child sits far from the pivot (1.5 m) and the heavier 450 N child sits closer (1.0 m). The anticlockwise moment (300 × 1.5 = 450 N·m) exactly balances the clockwise moment (450 × 1.0 = 450 N·m).

sections.title: Mistakes students often make
sections.body:
- **Checking only forces.** Balanced forces are not enough; the **moments must balance too**, or the object will spin.
- **Using the wrong distance.** Use the **perpendicular** distance from the pivot to the line of the force, not the slanted length.
- **Forgetting weight acts at the centre of mass.** A uniform beam's weight acts at its **midpoint**.
- **Thinking a couple has a net force.** A couple gives **pure rotation**; the two forces cancel, so there is no net force.
- **Choosing a poor pivot.** You can take moments about **any** point — pick one that makes an unknown force disappear (acts through the pivot).

sections.title: Tricks to remember it
sections.body:
- **"Two to balance":** forces balance **and** moments balance.
- **Principle of moments:** **"clockwise = anticlockwise."**
- **Seesaw rule:** heavier sits **closer**, lighter sits **further** (force × distance must match).
- **Couple = pure spin:** a steering wheel turned by two hands — turns but does not slide.
- Pick a clever pivot to **'hide' an unknown force** (let it act through the pivot so its moment is zero).

sections.title: Practice questions
sections.body:
Try these, then check the answers below.

**Q1.** A 200 N child sits 2.0 m from a pivot. What anticlockwise moment does she produce?

**Q2.** On a balanced beam, a 5.0 N weight is 0.40 m left of the pivot. A weight 0.20 m right of the pivot balances it. What is that weight?

**Q3.** A couple consists of two 8.0 N forces 0.50 m apart. What is the moment of the couple?

**Answers:**
- **A1.** `moment = F × d = 200 × 2.0 =` **400 N·m**.
- **A2.** `5.0 × 0.40 = W × 0.20` → `2.0 = 0.20 W` → W = **10 N**.
- **A3.** `moment = F × d = 8.0 × 0.50 =` **4.0 N·m**.

sections.title: Key points
sections.body:
- A particle is in **equilibrium** when the **net force is zero**.
- A rigid body needs **both**: `ΣF = 0` **and** `Στ = 0`.
- **Moment** = force × perpendicular distance from the pivot.
- **Principle of moments:** total clockwise moments = total anticlockwise moments.
- A **couple** is two equal, opposite, parallel forces giving **pure rotation**; its moment = force × distance between them.

chapters.title: Properties of Bulk Matter
chapters.description: The behaviour of solids, liquids and gases: elasticity and stress-strain, fluid statics (pressure and buoyancy), fluid dynamics, and heat and thermal expansion.

lessons.title: Elasticity, Fluids and Thermal Expansion
lessons.summary: Learn how solids stretch (stress, strain, Young's modulus), how fluids exert pressure and buoyancy, and how materials expand when heated.

sections.title: How matter behaves in bulk
sections.body:
Matter comes in **solids, liquids and gases**, and each behaves differently when you push, squeeze or heat it. A steel cable stretches a little under load; water pushes up on a boat; a metal bridge grows slightly longer on a hot day in Dire Dawa.

This lesson covers three big ideas about **bulk matter**: how solids deform (**elasticity**), how fluids exert pressure and lift (**fluid statics**), and how things change size with temperature (**thermal expansion**).

sections.title: What you will be able to do
sections.body:
By the end of this lesson you should be able to:

- Define **stress**, **strain** and **Young's modulus**.
- State **Hooke's law** for elastic materials.
- Calculate **pressure** in a fluid and explain **buoyancy** (Archimedes' principle).
- Explain the **continuity** idea in flowing fluids.
- Calculate **linear thermal expansion**.

sections.title: Elasticity, fluids and heat
sections.body:
**Elastic behaviour.** When you stretch a solid, it resists. **Stress** is the force per unit area: `stress = F / A` (in pascals, Pa). **Strain** is the fractional change in length: `strain = ΔL / L` (no units). For small loads, **Hooke's law** holds: stress is proportional to strain. The constant of proportionality is the **Young's modulus**:
`E = stress / strain = (F/A) / (ΔL/L)`
A large E means a stiff material (like steel). *Why a limit?* Beyond the **elastic limit** the material no longer returns to its original shape — it is permanently deformed.

**Fluid statics — pressure.** A fluid pushes on every surface it touches. **Pressure** is force per unit area: `P = F / A`. The pressure due to a column of fluid of depth h is:
`P = ρ g h`
where ρ (rho) is the density, g = 9.81 m/s², and h the depth. *Why depth matters:* deeper fluid has more weight above it pressing down, so the pressure is greater — this is why a dam is built thicker at the bottom.

**Buoyancy — Archimedes' principle.** Any object in a fluid feels an upward **buoyant force** equal to the **weight of the fluid it displaces**:
`F_buoyant = ρ_fluid × V_displaced × g`
This is why a boat floats: it sinks until it pushes aside a weight of water equal to its own weight.

**Fluid dynamics — continuity.** For a fluid flowing through a pipe that gets narrower, the fluid must speed up so the same amount passes each second: `A₁v₁ = A₂v₂`. *Why:* the fluid is (almost) incompressible, so what goes in must come out. This is why a river flows faster where it narrows.

**Thermal expansion.** Most materials **expand when heated** because their particles vibrate more and push apart. For a solid rod, the increase in length is:
`ΔL = α L ΔT`
where α (alpha) is the **coefficient of linear expansion**, L the original length, and ΔT the temperature rise. *Why it matters:* engineers leave **expansion gaps** in bridges and railway lines so they do not buckle in the heat.

sections.title: Worked example: thermal expansion of a steel rail
sections.body:
**Problem:** A steel railway rail is **20.0 m** long at 10 °C. On a hot day its temperature rises to **40 °C**. The coefficient of linear expansion of steel is **α = 1.2 × 10⁻⁵ /°C**. How much does the rail expand?

**Step 1 — Find the temperature change.**
`ΔT = 40 − 10 = 30 °C`

**Step 2 — Use the linear expansion formula.**
`ΔL = α L ΔT`
`ΔL = (1.2 × 10⁻⁵) × 20.0 × 30`

**Step 3 — Calculate.**
`ΔL = 1.2 × 10⁻⁵ × 600 = 7.2 × 10⁻³ m = 0.0072 m`

**Answer:** The rail expands by **7.2 mm**.

**Check:** Although 7.2 mm is small, over many joined rails it adds up — which is exactly why small **expansion gaps** are left between rails to prevent buckling.

sections.title: Mistakes students often make
sections.body:
- **Confusing stress and strain.** Stress is force per area (Pa); strain is the **fractional** change in length (no units).
- **Thinking pressure depends on the amount of water.** Fluid pressure depends on **depth**, not on the total volume or the width of the container.
- **Getting buoyancy backward.** The buoyant force equals the weight of the **fluid displaced**, not the weight of the object.
- **Forgetting to use a temperature change.** Expansion uses **ΔT** (the change), not the temperature itself.
- **Using the wrong area.** In P = F/A and stress = F/A, A is the area the force acts **over**, perpendicular to the force.

sections.title: Tricks to remember it
sections.body:
- **"Stress is the cause, strain is the change."** Stress = F/A (the push), strain = ΔL/L (the stretch).
- **"Deeper = harder push":** P = ρgh, so pressure grows with depth.
- **Archimedes in the bath:** the upthrust equals the weight of fluid **pushed aside**.
- **"Hot stuff grows":** ΔL = αLΔT — heat makes things expand.
- **Narrow = fast:** in a pipe, where it narrows the fluid speeds up (continuity).

sections.title: Practice questions
sections.body:
Try these, then check the answers below.

**Q1.** A force of 500 N acts on an area of 0.25 m². What is the pressure?

**Q2.** What is the water pressure at a depth of 10 m? (ρ = 1000 kg/m³, g = 9.81 m/s².)

**Q3.** An aluminium rod 2.0 m long is heated by 50 °C. If α = 2.3 × 10⁻⁵ /°C, how much does it expand?

**Answers:**
- **A1.** `P = F/A = 500 / 0.25 =` **2000 Pa**.
- **A2.** `P = ρgh = 1000 × 9.81 × 10 =` **98 100 Pa** (about 98 kPa).
- **A3.** `ΔL = αLΔT = 2.3 × 10⁻⁵ × 2.0 × 50 =` **2.3 × 10⁻³ m** (2.3 mm).

sections.title: Key points
sections.body:
- **Stress** = F/A; **strain** = ΔL/L; **Young's modulus** E = stress/strain measures stiffness.
- **Hooke's law:** stress ∝ strain up to the **elastic limit**.
- Fluid **pressure** `P = ρgh` increases with depth.
- **Archimedes' principle:** buoyant force = weight of fluid displaced.
- **Continuity:** `A₁v₁ = A₂v₂` — fluids speed up in narrower pipes.
- **Linear expansion:** `ΔL = αLΔT`; engineers leave expansion gaps.
